title: Times tables for 2, 5 and 10
keyIdea: A times table fact like 5 × 3 = 15 tells you how many are in equal groups. The 10s facts all end in 0. The 5s facts are half of the 10s facts. The 2s facts are doubles. Each times fact gives a division fact too: 5 × 3 = 15, so 15 ÷ 5 = 3 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Those facts make a fact family.
familyTip: Play 'fact ping-pong' on a walk. You say a 2s, 5s or 10s fact, like 5 × 4 = 20. Your child bats back a division fact from the same family: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 or 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Use real things too: count 10p coins, fingers on hands, or wheels on bikes.

visual.caption: Is each number in the 5 times table? Drag each card, or tap it then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: make 6 × 10 with 10p coins, cut tens in half to find 5 × 6, park bikes for 2 × 7, fill a fact family, and cover a corner to find division facts.

kid: A times fact tells you how many are in equal groups. 4 × 5 means 4 groups of 5. That makes 20. If you know it by heart, you do not need to count.
The 10s are easy to spot. 3 × 10 = 30 and 7 × 10 = 70. They all end in 0.
The 5s are half of the 10s. 10 × 6 = 60, so 5 × 6 = 30. The 5s end in 5 or 0. The 2s are doubles. 2 × 8 is 8 + 8, which is 16.

One fact gives you more. 5 × 3 = 15, so 3 × 5 = 15 too. You can also go back: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5. These four facts are a fact family. Take care: 15 ÷ 5 asks how many 5s make 15. It is not 15 take away 5.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. The National Curriculum in England, Year 2 Number (multiplication and division), asks pupils to recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, to recognise odd and even numbers, and to show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) while division cannot. Year 1 counting in 2s, 5s and 10s comes first.

The aim is recall, not counting up each time. Three links help. Multiples of 10 end in 0. Multiples of 5 are half the matching multiple of 10, so they end in 5 or 0. Multiples of 2 are doubles, and are the even numbers. Division facts come from the inverse: a fact family is three numbers, the product and two factors, giving two multiplication facts and two division facts.

Common mistakes: adding instead of multiplying (5 × 4 = 9); writing the digits side by side (10 × 8 = 108); for division, subtracting (30 ÷ 5 = 25) or multiplying (16 ÷ 2 = 32); thinking 15 ÷ 5 and 5 ÷ 15 are the same because 5 × 3 and 3 × 5 are; and counting from 1 on fingers every time, which is slow and slips.

In the lab your child adds 10p coins until 6 × 10 = 60, cuts six tens sticks in half to see that 5 × 6 = 30 is half of 60, parks seven bikes to see 2 × 7 = 14 as double 7, fills the four facts of the 3, 5, 15 family, and hides a corner of a triangle to find 20 ÷ 2, 50 ÷ 10 and 35 ÷ 5.

practice.hint: Think of 4 hands. Each hand has 5 fingers.
practice.explain: 4 groups of 5 is 20. 9 is 5 + 4, which adds instead of multiplying.

practice.prompt: There are {n} boxes. Each box holds 10 pencils. How many pencils?
practice.hint: This is {n} × 10. The 10s facts end in 0.

practice.prompt: {n} children each have 2 shoes on. How many shoes?
{=5*n} sweets are shared into bags of 5. How many bags?
practice.hint: How many 5s make {=5*n}? Use a 5s fact.

practice.prompt: 2 × 10 = 20. Which fact is in the same fact family?
practice.hint: A fact family uses the same three numbers: 2, 10 and 20.
practice.explain: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 undoes 2 × 10 = 20. The other two facts add or take away, so they are not in the family.

pool.hint: 8 groups of ten. The 10s facts end in 0.
pool.explain: 10 × 8 = 80. 18 adds the numbers, and 108 just writes them side by side.

pool.hint: 5 is half of 10, so the answer is half of 70.
pool.explain: Half of 70 is 35, so 5 × 7 = 35. 65 takes away 5, and 140 doubles instead of halving.
10 × {n} = {=10*n}, and half of that is {=5*n}. So 5 × {n} = {=5*n}.

pool.prompt: Which number is in the 5 times table?
pool.hint: Numbers in the 5s table end in 5 or 0.
pool.explain: 45 = 5 × 9, and it ends in 5. 52 and 28 end in 2 and 8, so they are not in the 5s table.

pool.prompt: The numbers 4, 10 and 40 make a fact family. Which fact is NOT in it?
pool.hint: In a division fact from this family, you start with the biggest number.
pool.explain: 40 ÷ 4 = 10 and 10 × 4 = 40 are in the family. Division does not work in any order, so 4 ÷ 40 is not 10.

pool.prompt: Sam says 2 × 9 is 11. What did Sam do?
pool.explain: 2 + 9 = 11, so Sam added. 2 × 9 is double 9, which is 18.
